dehydrated_text:
So now the Esso is pissed off at Jacob. So Jacob has no choice but to run away. He runs away and meets a relative. And what follows next is the greatest love story in the Bible, or perhaps the greatest love story ever in human history. The story is amazing because it is simple yet complex. Laban, who is a relative, says to Jacob, "You're my kinsman; should you therefore serve me for nothing? Tell me what shall your wages be?"

So, Jacob runs away from his brother and finds safety with Laban. He offers to work for Laban, but Laban says, "Listen, I can't just enslave you. So, you work for me and I'll give you whatever you want." Laban has two daughters: the elder was Leah, and the younger was Rachel. Leah's eyes were lovely, and Rachel was graceful and beautiful. Jacob loved Rachel so much that he said, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel." Laban agreed, saying it is better that he gives her to Jacob than anyone else.

Jacob serves seven years for Rachel, but when morning comes, it is Leah. Jacob says to Leah, "What have you done to me? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why then have you deceived me?" Laban explains that in their culture, the younger daughter should be married first, so he gives Rachel to Jacob after a week with Leah.

Jacob marries Rachel and loves her more than Leah. He serves Laban for another seven years. Clearly, Laban deceived Jacob. The question is why he did so. It turns out Rachel and Leah are sisters who hate each other; they are in competition. When Jacob says he loves Rachel, Leah becomes angry. For seven years, she pesters her father to let her be married first. Laban tricks Jacob by giving him Leah first and then Rachel.

Rachel loves Jacob but had to wait seven years before marrying him. Every day, Leah probably said to Rachel, "See, Jacob doesn't really love you." However, both endured the humiliation to stay together. This love story is a beautiful testament to the power of enduring hardship for love. The Bible, written by someone who clearly understands human emotions and relationships, captures this complexity with economy and irony.
